expectedText:
TERMINATION / SEPARATION LETTER
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

NOTICE OF TERMINATION
Acme, Inc. is ending Jordan Lee's employment with the company, effective September 30, 2026.

FINAL PAY
State law, not a single federal rule, controls when Jordan Lee's final paycheck is due. Some states require it immediately or within a few days of discharge; others allow payment on the next regularly scheduled payday. Which timeline applies depends on the state where Jordan Lee works.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "If an employer discharges an employee, the wages earned and unpaid at the time of discharge are due and payable immediately."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 201(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=201.)
  "If employment is terminated, the employer shall pay the wages not later than the regular pay day for the pay period during which the termination occurred, as established in accordance with the provisions of this section."
  — N.Y. Labor Law § 191(3) (New York State Senate text), New York Labor Law (https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/LAB/191)
  Known gap: This clause illustrates the range with two real, verified examples rather than surveying all fifty states — one state requires immediate payment on discharge, another allows payment on the next regular payday, and even the stricter of the two has its own narrow industry-specific carve-out. Which rule actually applies to a given final-pay date depends on the specific state, which this document doesn't determine.

CONTINUATION OF HEALTH COVERAGE (COBRA)
If Acme, Inc. offers a group health plan, Jordan Lee's termination is generally a “qualifying event” that gives Jordan Lee the right to continue that coverage at their own cost for up to 18 months, under the federal law known as COBRA — unless the termination was for gross misconduct. Acme, Inc. (or its plan administrator) must notify the plan of the qualifying event, which starts the clock on Jordan Lee's own notice of their continuation-coverage rights.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "The termination (other than by reason of such employee's gross misconduct), or reduction of hours, of the covered employee's employment."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1163(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, COBRA qualifying events (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1163)
  "the employer of an employee under a plan must notify the administrator of a qualifying event described in paragraph (1), (2), (4), or (6) of section 1163 of this title within 30 days (or, in the case of a group health plan which is a multiemployer plan, such longer period of time as may be provided in the terms of the plan) of the date of the qualifying event"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1166(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, COBRA notice requirements (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1166)
  "Subsection (a) shall not apply to any group health plan for any calendar year if all employers maintaining such plan normally employed fewer than 20 employees on a typical business day during the preceding calendar year."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1161(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, COBRA small-employer exception (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1161)
  "The coverage must extend for at least the period beginning on the date of the qualifying event and ending not earlier than the earliest of the following: (A) Maximum required period (i) General rule for terminations and reduced hours In the case of a qualifying event described in section 1163(2) of this title, except as provided in clause (ii), the date which is 18 months after the date of the qualifying event."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1162(2)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, COBRA maximum coverage period (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1162)
  Known gap: COBRA's continuation-coverage requirement generally does not apply to small employers — plans maintained by employers that normally had fewer than 20 employees in the prior calendar year are excepted. Some states have their own “mini-COBRA” laws extending similar rights to employees of smaller employers; those aren't covered here. Whether this particular termination genuinely qualifies as “gross misconduct” — the one exception named in the statute itself — is a fact-specific question this clause doesn't resolve. The 18-month figure in the body is the general-rule maximum for a termination-based qualifying event; it can extend to 36 months if a second qualifying event happens during that window, and runs on a different clock entirely for a qualifying event tied to bankruptcy proceedings. This clause states the general rule, not every extension scenario.

ACCRUED VACATION / PTO
Whether Jordan Lee is owed a payout for unused, accrued vacation or PTO at termination depends on the state and the terms of Acme, Inc.'s own policy. Some states treat earned vacation time as wages that vest as they're earned — once vested, it can't be forfeited, and must be paid out at termination. Many other states don't require any such payout at all, leaving it entirely to the employer's own policy.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "The right to a paid vacation, when offered in an employer's policy or contract of employment, constitutes deferred wages for services rendered. Case law from this state and others, as well as principles of equity and justice, compel the conclusion that a proportionate right to a paid vacation "vests" as the labor is rendered. Once vested, the right is protected from forfeiture, by section 227.3. On termination of employment, therefore, the statute requires that an employee be paid in wages for a pro rata share of his vacation pay."
  — Suastez v. Plastic Dress-Up Co., 31 Cal. 3d 774 (1982) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1173656/suastez-v-plastic-dress-up-co/)
  "Unless otherwise provided by a collective-bargaining agreement, whenever a contract of employment or employer policy provides for paid vacations, and an employee is terminated without having taken off his vested vacation time, all vested vacation shall be paid to him as wages at his final rate in accordance with such contract of employment or employer policy respecting eligibility or time served; provided, however, that an employment contract or employer policy shall not provide for forfeiture of vested vacation time upon termination."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 227.3 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=227.3)
  "However, an employment agreement may provide that the employee does not earn additional paid vacation if a specified amount of vested vacation remains unused. Such a provision does not attempt forfeiture of vested vacation and is therefore permissible."
  — Boothby v. Atlas Mechanical, Inc., 6 Cal. App. 4th 1595 (1992) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2297663/boothby-v-atlas-mechanical-inc/)
  Known gap: This clause draws on one state's verified, strict version of the no-forfeiture rule as real supporting evidence that this approach exists — not a claim about the company's actual state or policy. Whether any accrued time is owed here depends on which state's law applies and what the company's own written policy says, including whether it distinguishes vacation from other forms of paid time off. One distinction worth being precise about: even where a no-forfeiture rule applies, it bars taking away vacation already earned, but it does not require unlimited accrual — a policy that simply stops the clock on earning more once a specified amount is banked (an accrual cap, not a forfeiture of time already earned) is generally permitted. This clause's "can't be forfeited" language is about time already earned; it doesn't mean the company's policy has to let vacation accrue without limit.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge receipt of this letter.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
